sampleAnswers.answer: Annual leave is paid leave for rest that accrues progressively over a period of ongoing employment. Under the National Employment Standards, it does not apply to casual employees. Personal/carer's leave is paid leave for an employee's own illness or injury, or to care for a family or household member who needs care because of illness, injury or an emergency. sampleAnswers.answer:
Each type of leave in the scenario has a distinct purpose. Annual leave exists so that the employee can rest and recover from work, and the officer's planned holiday is its clearest use.

Parental leave has a different purpose: to support a parent to care for a new child during the early months of the child's life. The officer's child is due in four months, so this leave supports the transition to parenthood rather than rest, and the employer must not penalise the employee for taking it.

Family and domestic violence leave has a purpose of safety and access to support. The officer may need time for court attendances and medical appointments, and this leave recognises that a person should not have to lose their job to protect themselves or their children.

These purposes differ in their timing and in whether the leave is paid. Annual leave is planned and paid, parental leave is planned around a birth and is unpaid under the National Employment Standards, and family and domestic violence leave responds to an urgent need and is paid, up to 10 days in each 12-month period.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the purpose of three types of leave, applies each to the scenario, and explains why the purposes differ in timing and payment.

dotPoints.description: The regulatory framework for leave entitlements

prompts.question: Explain the regulatory framework for leave entitlements that applies to employees covered by the national workplace relations system.
markerNotes: Reward the layered structure: a national minimum, which awards and agreements can improve but not reduce.
Credit recognition that some leave, such as long service leave, depends largely on state or territory law.
Strong answers name the bodies that enforce leave entitlements and what each does.
commonStudentErrors: Describing leave as set only by modern awards
Treating the National Employment Standards as optional minimums that employers can waive in a contract
Overlooking state law as a source of long service leave
prompts.markingCriteria:

3 marks: Explains two sources of leave entitlements accurately, with limited detail on enforcement
2 marks: Identifies one source of leave entitlements accurately
1 mark: Makes a general statement that leave is regulated by law

sampleAnswers.answer: The regulatory framework for leave entitlements is built on several layers. The National Employment Standards in the Fair Work Act 2009 set a minimum floor of leave entitlements, including annual leave, personal and carer's leave and parental leave, which an employment contract cannot reduce. Modern awards and enterprise agreements may add to these entitlements. Long service leave is largely governed by state and territory law, and enforcement is shared between the Fair Work Ombudsman, which investigates breaches, and the Fair Work Commission, which resolves disputes. Employers and employees can check their obligations against the information that the Fair Work Ombudsman publishes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the layered framework from the National Employment Standards to awards and agreements, identifies state law for long service leave, and names the enforcement bodies.

sampleAnswers.answer: The National Employment Standards set minimum leave entitlements under the Fair Work Act. Modern awards and enterprise agreements can provide additional leave.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 3-mark response explains two sources of leave entitlements accurately, with no detail on enforcement or state law.

sampleAnswers.answer: Leave is regulated by law.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response makes a general statement without identifying a source of leave entitlements.

prompts.question: Analyse how the National Employment Standards and enterprise agreements interact to determine the leave entitlements of an employee within the regulatory framework.
markerNotes: Reward the identification that the manager's statement misreads the framework, because agreements may provide more than the minimum.
Credit reference to the approval of agreements and the better off overall test as the safeguard against reductions.
Strong answers explain what a leave loading is and why it is usually set by an award or agreement.
commonStudentErrors: Accepting the manager's statement that an agreement cannot give more leave than the National Employment Standards
Describing the National Employment Standards and agreements separately without analysing their relationship
Confusing a leave loading with a casual loading
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of how the National Employment Standards operate as a floor that enterprise agreements can improve but not reduce, explains the effect of the manager's statement in the scenario, and considers the approval and enforcement processes, reaching a supported conclusion
5-6 marks: Analyses the relationship between the National Employment Standards and enterprise agreements with accurate reasoning and some application to the scenario
3-4 marks: Describes the National Employment Standards and enterprise agreements with limited analysis of how they interact
1-2 marks: Makes a basic statement about leave entitlements

sampleAnswers.answer:
The regulatory framework for leave entitlements works as a floor: enterprise agreements may improve on it but cannot go below it. The National Employment Standards set the minimum leave that a permanent employee must receive, including annual leave and personal leave, and they apply regardless of what an employment contract says.

The human resources manager in the scenario is wrong to say that an enterprise agreement cannot give more leave than the National Employment Standards. An agreement is designed to improve on the minimum, so the agreement in the scenario can lawfully give extra annual leave and a leave loading, provided it has been approved. The error matters because an employee who relies on the statement may accept less than the agreement entitles them to.

The leave loading illustrates how agreements add to the framework. A loading is an additional payment, commonly made when annual leave is taken, and it is usually set by an award or agreement rather than by the standards themselves. Because it is an agreed term, the employer must pay it, and the employee can seek enforcement through the Fair Work Ombudsman if it is withheld.

Approval and enforcement connect the layers. The Fair Work Commission must be satisfied that an agreement passes the better off overall test before approving it, and the Fair Work Ombudsman investigates breaches of leave entitlements under the standards, awards and agreements.

On balance, the standards set the floor and agreements can improve on it. The manager's statement misreads that relationship, and a correct understanding is needed for the employee to receive the leave the agreement gives.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: analyses the floor and the bargaining layer, explains why the manager's statement is wrong, explains the leave loading and the approval and enforcement safeguards, and reaches a supported conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: The National Employment Standards set minimum leave entitlements that apply to every eligible employee. Enterprise agreements can provide more leave, such as a leave loading, so the manager's claim that agreements cannot improve on the standards is incorrect.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 5-mark response analyses the floor and the bargaining layer with accurate reasoning and some application, but does not consider the approval safeguard in depth.

sampleAnswers.answer: Leave is set by the National Employment Standards and by enterprise agreements.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response makes a basic statement about the two sources without analysing how they interact.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A permanent employee at a manufacturing firm is covered by an enterprise agreement that gives extra annual leave and a leave loading. The firm's human resources manager tells the employee that an enterprise agreement cannot give more leave than the National Employment Standards.

dotPoints.description: Measures to address a changing and diverse workforce without paid leave entitlements

prompts.question: Describe two measures that address the needs of a changing and diverse workforce without paid leave entitlements.
markerNotes: Accept casual loading and portable leave schemes as the main measures, and credit any other accurate measure that is explained.

3 marks: Describes two measures accurately, with limited explanation of how they support workers
2 marks: Describes one measure accurately

sampleAnswers.answer: Two measures address the needs of a changing and diverse workforce that is engaged without paid leave entitlements. The first is casual loading. Casual employees do not accrue paid leave, so awards and agreements usually pay a loading on top of the hourly rate to compensate them for the absence of paid leave and of guaranteed hours. The second is portable leave schemes in some industries. Where a worker moves between employers within the industry, the scheme carries accrued long service leave forward, which helps workers who change jobs frequently.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes two measures accurately, explains how each compensates for the absence of paid leave, and links both to a changing workforce.

sampleAnswers.answer: Casual loading is paid to casual employees instead of paid leave. Portable long service leave schemes in some industries let workers carry their entitlements between employers.

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of measures that protect workers without paid leave entitlements in a changing and diverse workforce.
markerNotes: Reward evaluation that separates pay compensation from time away from work, since a loading does not give a worker leave when they are ill.
Credit the point that workers classified as contractors generally lack the statutory leave protections, so the measures depend on classification.
Strong answers judge which further measures would close the gap in the scenario, and why.
commonStudentErrors: Treating casual loading as equivalent to paid leave
Assuming that portable schemes cover every industry and every worker
Overlooking the effect of employment classification on the rideshare driver
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained evaluation of how far the existing measures protect workers without paid leave, weighing casual loading, portable schemes and the position of contractors, and reaches a supported judgement about what further measures the scenario needs
6 marks: Evaluates the effectiveness of at least two measures with reasoning and application to the scenario
5 marks: Evaluates one measure and one limitation, with some application
3-4 marks: Describes measures with limited evaluation of their effectiveness

1 mark: Makes a general statement about leave for workers

sampleAnswers.answer:
The effectiveness of measures for workers without paid leave entitlements depends on whether they compensate for the lack of leave in a way that workers can rely on. Casual loading is the main protection for the hospitality workers in the scenario, but it is only effective if the loading is actually paid and hours are recorded accurately. Portable schemes and statutory minimums play complementary roles, but they do not reach every worker, which limits their effectiveness in a changing and diverse workforce.

Casual loading has the advantage of simplicity. A higher hourly rate is paid in place of paid leave, so the worker receives value without having to claim anything. However, it does not provide time away from work, so a worker who is ill or needs time for family responsibilities has no paid leave to draw on.

Portable schemes address the difficulty of accruing entitlements when a worker moves between employers, carrying forward leave within an industry. Their effectiveness depends on whether the worker is covered, and the scenario does not show that the hospitality or fitness workers are covered by such a scheme.

The rideshare driver illustrates the limit of these measures most clearly. A worker engaged as an independent contractor generally has no statutory right to paid sick leave, and the injury leaves the driver without income for three weeks. Measures that depend on employment status cannot protect such a worker, so effectiveness depends on classification as much as on the leave measures themselves.

On balance, the measures are partly effective for workers without paid leave entitlements. Casual loading and portable schemes give real but uneven protection, and the lack of leave for contractors leaves a significant gap. Effectiveness would increase if loadings were enforced consistently and if app-based workers had minimum protections when injured.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a sustained evaluation of casual loading, portable schemes and the contractor gap, applied to the three workplaces, and a supported judgement about the further measures needed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Casual loading gives workers a higher hourly rate in place of paid leave, which is simple and immediate. However, it gives no time away from work when a worker is ill, so it protects pay but not health or family responsibilities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 5-mark response evaluates one measure and one limitation, with some application, but does not evaluate the portable schemes or the contractor position.

dotPoints.description: The need to protect workers’ rights regarding discrimination and termination

prompts.question: Explain why the law must protect workers' rights regarding discrimination and termination, using the scenario.
markerNotes: Reward the explanation of the power imbalance: an employer decides hiring, hours and continued employment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Workers' rights regarding discrimination and termination need legal protection because the employment relationship involves a clear imbalance of power. An employer decides how hours are allocated and whether employment continues, so a worker treated unfairly has little practical means of resisting. Discrimination on grounds such as family responsibilities undermines the dignity and equality of the worker, and losing a job can cause serious economic hardship. In the scenario, the retail worker who asked for a flexible roster to care for her child was cut back and dismissed, which shows why this protection matters.

prompts.question: Justify the view that protecting workers from unlawful discrimination and unlawful termination is essential to the protection of human rights.
markerNotes: Reward a clear position supported by reasons, and a counterargument that is answered rather than merely stated.
Credit the link between economic security and the right to work, and between equality and protection against discriminatory dismissal.
Do not accept that an international declaration is a treaty that binds every state in the same way as a convention.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a position without reasons drawn from human rights instruments
Treating a declaration as a binding treaty
Failing to answer the counterargument about employer flexibility
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a clear position that protection from unlawful discrimination and termination is essential to human rights, supported by at least two reasons drawn from international instruments such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and ILO conventions, and recognises a limit or counterargument, such as the employer's interest in managing its workforce
5 marks: Justifies the position with two reasons accurately explained
4 marks: Justifies the position with one reason accurately explained
3 marks: States a position with limited reasoning
2 marks: Identifies one reason with minimal support
1 mark: Makes a general statement about human rights at work

sampleAnswers.answer:
Protecting workers from unlawful discrimination and unlawful termination is essential to human rights because a person's livelihood is closely tied to their dignity, security and ability to take part in society. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights recognises the right to work and to protection against unemployment, and an unlawful termination directly undermines those rights.

The first reason is economic security. A worker dismissed for an unlawful reason, such as their sex, race, disability or a complaint, loses income and may lose housing, health cover and the community that work provides.

The second reason is equality. Unlawful termination is often a form of discrimination, in which a worker is removed because of a protected characteristic. The International Labour Organization's conventions on discrimination in employment recognise that equal opportunity at work is a human right.

A counterargument is that employers need flexibility to manage their workforce and respond to poor performance. This concern is legitimate, but a valid reason does not justify termination for discriminatory or retaliatory motives. Protection is therefore a limit on arbitrary termination rather than a denial of the employer's ability to manage the business.

On balance, protecting workers from unlawful termination is essential to human rights because it secures the economic security, dignity and equality that the right to work is meant to guarantee.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: takes a clear position, supports it with reasons on economic security and equality drawn from human rights instruments, and answers the counterargument about employer flexibility.

sampleAnswers.answer: Protecting workers from unlawful termination protects their economic security, because losing a job for an unlawful reason can cause hardship. Human rights instruments recognise the right to work and protection against unemployment, so the protection is part of those rights.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response justifies the position with one reason, economic security, linked to human rights instruments, but does not develop a second reason or address a counterargument.

sampleAnswers.answer: Workers have a human right to work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies one reason with minimal support.

prompts.question: Describe two laws that regulate unlawful workplace discrimination in Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two Commonwealth laws regulate unlawful workplace discrimination. The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) makes it unlawful to treat a person less favourably because of sex, pregnancy or family responsibilities, including in recruitment, promotion and dismissal. The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth) makes it unlawful to discriminate because of disability, and a failure to make reasonable adjustments can itself be discrimination unless the adjustment would impose unjustifiable hardship. A worker who believes either Act has been breached can usually complain to the relevant commission. Both Acts operate alongside state law such as the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW), so a worker may have options under more than one law.

prompts.question: Analyse how the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) protects employees from unfair dismissal and unlawful termination.
markerNotes: Reward the distinction between a test of the fairness of a dismissal and a test of the reason for it.
Credit the point that a restructure must be genuine, and that a claimed restructure which removes no other positions is weak evidence.
Strong answers note the practical requirements for each route, including a minimum period of employment and a time limit for making a claim.
commonStudentErrors: Treating unfair dismissal and general protections as the same claim
Accepting the employer's restructure explanation without testing it
Overlooking that a complaint about a workplace right can ground a general protections claim
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of the two protections, explaining that unfair dismissal tests whether a dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable, while the general protections test whether the dismissal was for a prohibited reason, and applies both to the scenario, including the restructure explanation
5-6 marks: Analyses the unfair dismissal and general protection provisions with accurate reasoning and some application to the scenario
3-4 marks: Describes the protections with limited analysis of how they apply
1-2 marks: Makes a basic statement about dismissal laws

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) protects employees from unfair dismissal and unlawful termination through two related but different routes. The unfair dismissal provisions ask whether a dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable, taking into account whether there was a valid reason related to conduct or capacity, whether the employee was notified and given a chance to respond, and the size of the employer. The general protections provisions prohibit adverse action, including dismissal, for a prohibited reason such as exercising a workplace right. One tests the fairness of the decision, while the other tests the reason for it.

The unfair dismissal route requires a minimum period of employment, and a claim must be made to the Fair Work Commission within 21 days after the dismissal took effect. The Commission considers the reasons for the dismissal and the process followed, and can order reinstatement or compensation if it finds the dismissal unfair. In the scenario, two years of service likely satisfies the minimum period, but the employer would still need a valid reason and a fair process.

The general protections route is directed at the reason for the dismissal rather than its fairness. The worker complained about unpaid overtime, which is an exercise of a workplace right, so the dismissal could be challenged even if it would otherwise be fair. The reason is presumed to be the complaint unless the employer proves otherwise.

The restructure explanation is relevant to both routes. A restructure supports a dismissal only if it is a genuine redundancy, meaning the employer no longer requires the job to be performed by anyone because of changes in its operational requirements, any consultation obligation has been met, and redeployment would not have been reasonable. The claim that no other positions were removed is therefore important evidence. If the restructure is a pretext, it is unlikely to protect the employer against either claim.

On balance, the worker can pursue both routes together or separately. Success depends on acting within the time limits and on obtaining the evidence needed to show the real reason for the dismissal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: distinguishes the unfair dismissal test from the general protections test, applies both to the complaint and the restructure explanation, and notes the practical requirements for each route.

sampleAnswers.answer: Unfair dismissal asks whether a dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable, while the general protections ask whether the dismissal was for a prohibited reason. A worker dismissed after complaining about unpaid overtime may have a claim under the general protections, even if the employer has a reason for the dismissal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 5-mark response analyses the two protections with accurate reasoning and some application, but does not test the restructure explanation or practical requirements.

sampleAnswers.answer: Unfair dismissal laws protect employees from being dismissed unfairly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response makes a basic statement about dismissal laws without analysis.

dotPoints.description: The roles of courts and tribunals in resolving disputes and imposing penalties, including alternative dispute resolution

prompts.question: Explain the roles of courts and tribunals in resolving employment disputes and imposing penalties, including alternative dispute resolution.
markerNotes: Reward the distinction between tribunals, which resolve disputes and can order remedies, and courts, which can impose civil penalties.
Credit the point that alternative dispute resolution is voluntary and that a mediated outcome is binding only once the parties agree.
Strong answers note that the Fair Work Commission cannot impose civil penalties, which are imposed by a court.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the Fair Work Commission can impose civil penalties
Describing mediation as a binding decision made by a mediator
Describing courts and tribunals without linking them to the scenario
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains the roles of courts and tribunals in resolving disputes and imposing penalties, including conciliation and arbitration by the Fair Work Commission, the power of courts to impose civil penalties and orders, and the role of alternative dispute resolution, applies these to the scenario and notes the trade-offs
5 marks: Explains the roles of at least two dispute bodies and one form of alternative dispute resolution accurately, with some application
4 marks: Explains the role of one tribunal or court and one form of alternative dispute resolution, with limited application
3 marks: Describes the role of courts or tribunals in general terms with some accuracy
2 marks: Identifies one dispute body or form of dispute resolution with minimal explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that disputes can be resolved

sampleAnswers.answer:
Courts and tribunals resolve employment disputes and impose penalties in different ways, and alternative dispute resolution can be quicker and less adversarial. The Fair Work Commission can conciliate disputes, helping the parties reach an agreed outcome, and can decide a matter by arbitration where the Act allows. In the scenario, the cleaner's unfair dismissal claim can go to the Commission, which can order reinstatement or compensation.

Courts have a different role, particularly in imposing penalties. Where an employer has breached workplace laws, such as by not paying penalty rates, a court such as the Federal Court may impose civil penalties and order the employer to pay the amounts owed. Penalties serve as a deterrent as well as a remedy for the worker.

Alternative dispute resolution, such as mediation, is private, flexible and often quicker. A mediator helps the parties negotiate a solution without deciding who is right. The advantage is that the parties keep control of the outcome, but a worker who needs a binding order may not obtain one through mediation.

The appropriate route depends on the type of dispute, the remedy the worker needs and the balance of power between the parties. In the scenario, the cleaner may benefit from conciliation, while the worker seeking penalties may need a court to enforce the law.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Fair Work Commission can conciliate an unfair dismissal claim, and it can order reinstatement or compensation in some cases. Courts can impose civil penalties for breaches of workplace laws, which act as a deterrent to employers.

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of alternative dispute resolution compared with the processes of courts and tribunals in resolving employment disputes.
markerNotes: Reward a comparison between the processes, not separate descriptions of each.
Credit recognition that mediation is voluntary and that an outcome binds only once agreed, which matters for an employee who needs an enforceable order.
Strong answers consider whether the employee's bargaining power and resources affect the fairness of the outcome.
commonStudentErrors: Describing alternative dispute resolution as always cheaper for everyone
Assuming that a mediated outcome is enforceable in the same way as a court order
Failing to judge which process is effective for the employee in the scenario
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained evaluation of how far alternative dispute resolution is effective compared with courts and tribunals, weighing speed, cost, confidentiality and the working relationship against enforceability, the balance of power and the remedies available, and reaches a supported judgement for the scenario

3-4 marks: Describes alternative dispute resolution and courts or tribunals with limited judgement about effectiveness

sampleAnswers.answer:
The effectiveness of alternative dispute resolution compared with courts and tribunals depends on what the parties need from the dispute. Alternative dispute resolution, such as mediation and conciliation, is usually faster, cheaper and more private, and it lets the parties shape an outcome that a tribunal could not order. Courts and tribunals produce binding decisions and enforceable remedies, but they are more formal, slower and more expensive.

Alternative dispute resolution is effective in several respects. A mediator can help the parties identify their interests and explore options such as a reference or a payment. Being voluntary and private, it can preserve the working relationship. For a long-serving employee, mediation may achieve a practical outcome more quickly than a hearing.

Its limits are significant in the scenario. A mediated outcome is binding only when the parties agree to it, so an employee who needs an enforceable order may not obtain one. The process also depends on bargaining power. A business owner with more resources may shape the outcome to favour the employer, and an employee with limited savings may feel pressure to accept a settlement.

A tribunal can decide whether a dismissal was unfair and order remedies such as reinstatement or compensation. However, the costs and time of a hearing may be a practical barrier for an employee without legal representation. The existence of a tribunal process still gives the employee a route that does not depend on the employer's willingness to settle, which can discourage a poor offer.

On balance, alternative dispute resolution is effective for many disputes, but courts and tribunals remain necessary where the employee needs an enforceable outcome and bargaining power is unequal. In the scenario, the sensible approach is to attend mediation with support while preserving the right to take the matter to the tribunal if the offer is unfair.

prompts.question: Explain two barriers that prevent workers from participating in employment dispute resolution.
markerNotes: Accept any two accurately explained barriers, and credit an explanation of why each barrier falls hardest on workers with low income or insecure work.
Reward the link between the barrier and the worker's inability to take part, not only the naming of the barrier.
Do not accept that a worker's lack of legal knowledge is a barrier only for workers who cannot read.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two barriers prevent many workers from participating in employment dispute resolution. The first is cost and access to legal help. Representation, and the time away from work needed to attend a conciliation or hearing, can be significant for a worker on a low income, so a worker may decide not to pursue a claim even where they have a strong case. The second is fear of reprisal. A worker who depends on the job may fear fewer shifts or dismissal if they raise a dispute, a fear that is especially strong for casual workers and may stop them starting the process at all.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains two barriers accurately, shows how each prevents a worker from taking part, and identifies why each falls hardest on insecure and low-income workers.

sampleAnswers.answer: Many workers cannot afford a lawyer, which can stop them from pursuing a claim. Fear of losing their job can also stop workers from raising a dispute.

sampleAnswers.answer: Some workers find disputes hard to pursue.

prompts.question: Analyse how barriers to participation in employment dispute resolution affect vulnerable workers and the effectiveness of workplace law.
markerNotes: Reward analysis of how barriers combine, for example fear of reprisal together with limited knowledge of the right body.
Credit the point that a protection that workers cannot practically use is less effective, however well drafted it is.
Strong answers note what would reduce the barriers, such as information in several languages and access to low-cost advice.
commonStudentErrors: Listing barriers without analysing how they combine or affect vulnerable workers
Concluding that workplace law is ineffective without evidence from the scenario
Overlooking fear of reprisal as a barrier where the legal protection exists
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of how barriers to participation, including cost, language, fear of reprisal, limited knowledge and time limits, prevent vulnerable workers from enforcing their rights, and evaluates the effect on the effectiveness of workplace law, applying this to the scenario
5-6 marks: Analyses at least two barriers with accurate examples and some application to vulnerable workers
3-4 marks: Describes barriers to dispute resolution with limited analysis of their effect
1-2 marks: Makes a basic statement about barriers facing workers

sampleAnswers.answer:
Barriers to participation in employment dispute resolution affect vulnerable workers because they prevent the people most exposed to unlawful treatment from using the protections the law provides. A workplace law that workers cannot practically enforce is less effective, however well drafted it is. In the scenario, the international students and the casual kitchen worker have been underpaid but have made no complaint, so the formal protections are not reaching them.

The first barrier is fear of reprisal. The students fear that a complaint could affect their visas, and the kitchen worker has been told that complaints are not welcome. This fear is strongest for casual and insecure workers, and it operates as a barrier even where the legal protection against adverse action exists.

The second barrier is language and knowledge. A worker who does not read English well may not understand their pay slip or the complaint process, and the kitchen worker does not know which body to contact. Information from the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Fair Work Commission must be accessible in the languages workers use.

The third barrier is cost and access to legal help. Representation is expensive and free legal services are limited, so a worker may decide that a claim is not worth pursuing. Time away from work to attend a conciliation or hearing is also a cost for a worker who depends on each shift. Some claims must also be made within short time limits, so delay can cost a worker the right to pursue a claim.

On balance, these barriers weaken the effectiveness of workplace law for vulnerable workers, because protections exist on paper but are not used in practice. Clear information in several languages, protection against reprisal that workers can rely on and access to low-cost advice would help the law reach the workers it is designed to protect, including those in the scenario.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a sustained analysis of fear of reprisal, language and knowledge, cost and time limits, applied to the students and the kitchen worker, and evaluates the effect on the effectiveness of workplace law.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fear of reprisal stops workers from complaining, even where the law protects them. Language barriers and limited knowledge of the right body can also keep vulnerable workers from enforcing their rights, so workplace law is less effective for them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Vulnerable workers can find it hard to make complaints.
